{{expert-subject|1=Mathematics|date=January 2014|reason=Needs to be checked by editor with advanced mathematics knowledge}}

In [[number theory]], '''Gillies' conjecture''' is a [[conjecture]] about the distribution of [[prime number|prime]] [[divisor|factors]] of [[Mersenne number]]s. It was made by [[Donald B. Gillies]] in a 1964 paper<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Gillies
| first = Donald B.
| authorlink = Donald B. Gillies
| title = Three new Mersenne primes and a statistical theory
| year = 1964
| journal = [[Mathematics of Computation]]
| volume = 18
| issue = 85
| pages = 93–97
| doi = 10.1090/S0025-5718-1964-0159774-6
}}</ref> in which he also announced the discovery of three new [[Mersenne prime]]s. The conjecture is a specialization of the [[prime number theorem]] and is a refinement of conjectures due to [[I. J. Good]]<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Good
| first = I. J.
| authorlink = I. J. Good
| title = Conjectures concerning the Mersenne numbers
| year = 1955
| journal = [[Mathematics of Computation]]
| volume = 9
| issue = 51
| pages = 120–121
| doi = 10.1090/S0025-5718-1955-0071444-6
}}</ref> and [[Daniel Shanks]].<ref>{{cite book
| last = Shanks
| first = Daniel
| authorlink = Daniel Shanks
| title = Solved and Unsolved Problems in Number Theory
| year = 1962
| publisher = Spartan Books
| location = [[Washington, D. C.|Washington]]
| pages = 198
}}</ref>

Several papers have given empirical support to the conjecture, but it disagrees with the widely accepted (but also open) [[Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff conjecture]].

==The conjecture==
Let <math>p</math> be a [[prime number]] and <math>M_p=2^p-1</math> the corresponding [[Mersenne prime]]. If <math>A < B < \sqrt{M_p}</math>, as <math>B/A</math> and <math>M_p \rightarrow \infty</math>, the number of prime divisors of <math>M</math> in the interval <math>[A, B]</math> is [[Poisson distribution|Poisson distributed]] with [[expected value]]
:<math>
\begin{cases}
\log(\log B /\log A) & \text{ if }A \geq 2p, \\[1pt]
\log(\log B/\log 2p) & \text{ if } A < 2p.
\end{cases}
</math>

The conjecture implies that
# The number of Mersenne primes less than <math>x</math> is asymptotically <math>\textstyle\frac{2\log\log x}{\log 2}</math>.
# The expected number of Mersenne primes <math>M_p</math> with <math>x \le p \le 2x</math> is <math>2</math>.
# The probability that <math>M_p</math> is prime is <math>\textstyle\frac{2 \log 2p }{p\log 2}</math>.

==Incompatibility with Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff conjecture==

The [[Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff conjecture]] gives different values:<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Wagstaff
| first = Samuel S.
| authorlink = Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr.
| title = Divisors of Mersenne numbers
| year = 1983
| journal = [[Mathematics of Computation]]
| volume = 40
| issue = 161
| pages = 385–397
| doi = 10.1090/S0025-5718-1983-0679454-X
}}</ref><ref name=heur>Chris Caldwell, [http://primes.utm.edu/mersenne/heuristic.html Heuristics: Deriving the Wagstaff Mersenne Conjecture]. Retrieved on 2017-07-26.</ref>
# The number of Mersenne primes less than <math>x</math> is asymptotically <math>\textstyle\frac{e^\gamma}{\log 2} \log\log x</math>.
# The expected number of Mersenne primes <math>M_p</math> with <math>x \le p \le 2x</math> is <math>e^\gamma</math>.
# The probability that <math>M_p</math> is prime is <math>\textstyle\frac{e^\gamma\log ap}{p\log 2}</math>, where <math>a=2</math> if <math>p=3 \!\!\pmod{4}</math> and <math>a=6</math> otherwise.

Asymptotically, these values are about 11% smaller.

==Results==
While Gillie's conjecture remains open, several papers have added empirical support to its validity.<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Ehrman
| first = John R.
| title = The number of prime divisors of certain Mersenne numbers
| year = 1967
| journal = [[Mathematics of Computation]]
| volume = 21
| issue = 100
| pages = 700–704
| doi = 10.1090/S0025-5718-1967-0223320-1
}}</ref>
